title: Break the Resistance: 5 Proactive Techniques for When Routines and High Expectations Aren’t Enough
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele picks up from his earlier pieces on routines and high expectations to address the students and classes that stay resistant even when a teacher has done everything by the book. He offers five proactive techniques: gathering lived insight from colleagues before reading dense SEN passports, a 30-second private doorway connection, analysing and managing peer dynamics through seating, tailoring the entry routine to where students have just come from, and planning for memory decay across long gaps between lessons. Each technique is paired with a short rationale and a research anchor such as Cornelius-White, Cook et al. on positive greetings at the door, Bandura, Cognitive Load Theory and the forgetting curve. He closes with a deliberately contrarian point that calling home is overrated when every individual teacher does it, and argues that persistent behavioural contact should be centralised through form tutors, heads of department, pastoral leads or SLT. The thread running through the piece is that prevention and relationship, not escalation, are the highest-return uses of a teacher’s limited time.
points: A three-minute conversation with a colleague who already has rapport with a student, asking about triggers and fastest de-escalation, can surface situational detail that formal SEN documentation misses.
Greeting a resistant student privately at the door before the lesson shifts the dynamic from public confrontation to private partnership and removes the peer audience.

Behaviour in the room should be planned around where students have just come from, using a silent lineup and retrieval starter after PE or active subjects and turn-and-talk after quiet desk-bound ones.
After a long gap between lessons, teachers should assume expectations and content have decayed and run a quick retrieval starter and re-model routines instead of punishing the regression.

Emanuele argues that individual teachers acting as isolated call centres is unsustainable, and that persistent behaviour contact home works better when centralised through tutors, pastoral leads or SLT.
quotes: When baseline routines hit a brick wall, you need high-leverage proactive strategies to prevent major escalations before they happen.

While formal SEN documentation provides vital statutory context and essential baseline strategies, it often lacks situational nuances. Human intelligence gives you actionable, lived insights that save weeks of trial and error.

It shifts the dynamic from public confrontation to private partnership. Meeting students at the threshold sets a supportive tone and removes the audience, drastically lowering defiancy driven by peer pressure.

Peer influence is one of the strongest drivers of secondary student behavior. Controlling the seating plan based on social observational data prevents group-mentality off-task behaviour before it starts.
Cognitive transition times are high-risk zones for behavioural disruption. Tailoring your entry routine to their immediate physical and mental state reduces friction.

Expecting students to maintain perfect behavioural and cognitive continuity over a 5-day gap leads to teacher frustration. Anticipating the regression allows you to remediate it intentionally rather than reactively punishing it.
Individual classroom teachers should not be expected to act as isolated call centers.
Use your time and energy where it has the highest ROI: proactive, relational, and structural techniques inside your classroom.
